title: Exercise 7C · Q5
summary: Expand a² + b² algebraically and show it always equals c².
alt: Exercise 7C · Q5: The lengths of the sides, a, b and c, of a triangle are given by a = m² − n², b = 2mn and c = m² + n², where m and n are positive integers and m > n. Show that the triangle is a right-angled triangle.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: A triangle has sides **a = m² − n²**, **b = 2mn** and **c = m² + n²**, where **m** and **n** are positive integers with **m > n**. Show that this triangle is **always** right-angled, whatever **m** and **n** are. (Shown here for **m = 2, n = 1**: a = 3, b = 4, c = 5.)

steps.title: Expand a² + b²
steps.narration: Start with **a² + b²** and expand both squares.\[\begin{aligned}a^2 + b^2 &= (m^2-n^2)^2 + (2mn)^2 \\ &= (m^4 - 2m^2n^2 + n^4) + 4m^2n^2\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Compare with c²
steps.narration: But **c = m² + n²**, so **(m² + n²)² = c²**.\[\begin{aligned}a^2 + b^2 &= c^2\end{aligned}\] Since **a² + b² = c²**, by the **Converse of Pythagoras' Theorem**, this triangle is **always** right-angled, with the right angle **opposite the side c**.

formulas.title: Pythagorean-triple generator
formulas.text: For any positive integers m > n, these three expressions always form a right-angled triangle.

challenges.title: Try m = 3, n = 2
challenges.prompt: If m = 3 and n = 2, find c = m² + n².

takeaways: This formula **generates a Pythagorean triple** for every choice of positive integers m > n.
The proof is pure **algebra** — expand, collect like terms, and recognise the perfect square.
m = 2, n = 1 gives the smallest triple, **3, 4, 5**.

notes.title: Try it yourself
notes.text: m = 3, n = 2 gives a = 5, b = 12, c = 13 — another famous triple, generated by the very same formula.
